title: Communication Protocols
intro: A communication protocol is the agreement that lets two devices exchange information over a wire, a radio link or a network. Both ends must agree on the physical connection, on when a value is valid, on how to find where one message starts and ends, and on what the values mean. If any one of those differs, the bits arrive but the information does not.

blocks.text: The four things a protocol fixes

items: Physical layer: the connector, the number of wires, the voltages that stand for 0 and 1 (or, for an analog signal, the range of the signal), and the impedance the line expects.
Timing: when the receiver should read the line. Either a clock travels with the data, or both ends agree on a rate in advance, or the clock is recovered from the data itself.
Framing: how the receiver finds the start of a unit, whether that is a byte (a start bit), a packet (a header) or a video line (a sync pulse).
Meaning: what the bytes, packets or voltage levels represent, such as a register address, a pixel brightness or the identity of the neuron that fired.

Serial or parallel. A serial link sends one bit after another on one wire or wire pair; a parallel link sends many bits at once on many wires. Parallel looks faster, but at high speed the wires drift out of step (skew), so modern fast links are serial.

Synchronous or asynchronous. A synchronous link shares a clock (SPI, I²C) or a timing reference (the sync pulses of VGA). An asynchronous link such as a UART shares no clock: both sides agree on a bit rate and resynchronise on every start bit.

Single-ended or differential. Single-ended signals are measured against ground. Differential signals use a pair of wires driven in opposite directions and the receiver reads the difference, which rejects noise picked up equally by both wires. USB, HDMI, Ethernet and CAN are differential.
Analog or digital. Most protocols carry bits. A few carry a continuously varying voltage: VGA's colour wires are analog, and the monitor turns each voltage straight into a brightness.
Point-to-point or bus. A point-to-point link joins exactly two devices. A bus shares the wires among many devices, so it needs addresses and a rule for who may talk (I²C addresses, CAN arbitration).
Streaming or packet-based. A stream sends data continuously at a fixed rhythm, like a video signal. A packet protocol sends self-contained messages with headers, like USB or Ethernet.

UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter): two signal wires, one each way, no clock. Each byte starts with a low start bit and ends with a high stop bit; 9,600 and 115,200 bits per second are common rates. The usual debug console on microcontrollers and FPGA boards.

SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface): a controller drives a clock line, data lines in each direction and one chip-select line per device. Full duplex, simple and fast (tens of MHz). Used for flash memory, displays, ADCs and SD cards.

I²C (Inter-Integrated Circuit): two shared open-drain wires, data (SDA) and clock (SCL), with pull-up resistors. Devices have 7-bit addresses; standard mode runs at 100 kbit/s and fast mode at 400 kbit/s. Used for sensors, configuration chips and the monitor-identification channel inside a VGA cable.
VGA: an analog video interface. Three colour voltages plus separate horizontal and vertical sync wires describe a picture one line at a time. See #/communication-protocols/vga.
DVI and HDMI: digital video sent as TMDS (transition-minimised differential signalling), with three data pairs and a clock pair; each 8-bit value travels as a 10-bit symbol.
USB: packets on a differential pair, scheduled by the host. The host polls devices; devices never talk unprompted.
CAN (controller area network): a differential bus for cars and machines. Any node may start sending; when two collide, the message with the lower identifier wins without either being corrupted.
Ethernet: frames with source and destination addresses and a checksum, over differential pairs or fibre.

blocks.text: Why protocols matter for building a brain

A spiking network is itself a communication system: neurons send short, all-or-nothing events, and what matters is which neuron fired and when. Neuromorphic chips carry spikes between cores and between chips with address-event representation (AER), a protocol in which each spike is a small packet holding the address of the neuron that fired, and the time of arrival is the time of the spike. See #/neuromorphic-hardware. At a higher level, the Thousand Brains Project's Monty system has columns exchange messages in a fixed format, the Cortical Messaging Protocol. See #/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/monty.

The practical side matters too. If you build a spiking network on an FPGA, you need a way to get data off the board: a UART to send numbers to a laptop, SPI or I²C to read a sensor, and a VGA output to draw a live spike raster on any spare monitor with nothing more than a few resistors. The VGA subtopic walks through that interface in detail.

A good habit when meeting a new protocol: ask the four questions above. What are the wires and levels? Where does the timing come from? How does the receiver find the start of a unit? What do the values mean? Every datasheet answers them, though rarely in that order.
